headline: Movement Grows to Abolish Alphabetical Order: 'Why Does A Get to Be First?'
subheadline: 847 signatories demand investigation into 'Big Alphabet' and historical letter favoritism
summary: A grassroots campaign questioning the arbitrary primacy of the letter A has gained surprising traction, with schools and libraries facing pressure to adopt alternative ordering systems.
content:
What started as a joke petition has evolved into a genuine movement: thousands of people are demanding to know why the alphabet is ordered the way it is, and whether it's time for a change.

'A has been first for over 3,000 years,' said movement organizer Tamara Wells. 'No elections. No rotation. No justification. A just... is first. Why? Because Phoenicians said so? This is 2024. We can do better.'

The 'Alphabetical Justice Coalition' has gathered 847 signatures demanding that schools and libraries investigate 'alternative ordering systems' that don't privilege certain letters over others. Their proposals include reverse alphabetical order, frequency-based ordering (with E taking its 'rightful place' at the top), and a rotating system where each letter gets to be first for one month.

'Think about the children whose names start with Z,' Wells continued. 'Their entire lives, they've been last in every roll call, every sorted list, every alphabetized arrangement. That's not just inconvenient. That's systematic letterism.'

Dr. James Chen, a linguist at Hartwell University, called the movement 'fascinating from a sociological standpoint, if not a practical one.'

'Alphabetical order is arbitrary,' Dr. Chen confirmed. 'There's no linguistic reason A should precede B. The order was essentially locked in by historical accident. But arbitrary doesn't mean changeable. The alphabet's ordering is now embedded in everything from database indexing to library systems. Changing it would be catastrophically impractical.'

This practical argument has not deterred supporters. A Threadit community, r/AlphabetAnarchy, has emerged dedicated to 'disrupting alphabetical hegemony.' Users post content deliberately sorted by alternative systems and celebrate any instance of non-alphabetical organization.

'I sorted my bookshelf by publication date,' wrote user u/ZFirstAlways. 'It felt revolutionary.'

Critics have mocked the movement as 'the most first-world problem imaginable.' Chirper users pointed out that the organizer's name, Tamara, benefits from a mid-alphabet position, leading to accusations of 'T privilege' and demands for disclosure of any potential letter-based conflicts of interest.

Wells dismissed the criticism. 'This isn't about me. This is about questioning the systems we take for granted. Today it's alphabetical order. Tomorrow, maybe we'll ask why weeks have seven days, or why we count in base ten. Everything is a construct. And constructs can be reconstructed.'

The campaign has launched a Chirper hashtag, #ShuffleTheAlphabet, which briefly trended before being overtaken by coverage of an unrelated celebrity scandal.
author: Marcus Webb, Trend Watch
